TROP implementations compared: the paper, Python, Stata and R

Source: vignettes/articles/implementation-comparison.Rmd
implementation-comparison.Rmd

The Triply RObust Panel (TROP) estimator of Athey, Imbens, Qu and Viviano (2026) is available in four places:

  • The paper, which defines the estimator, its weights and its leave-one-out cross-validation.
  • Python: the official trop package (zhaonanq/TROP-Estimator).
  • Stata: the official trop command (justinwaddy/TROP).
  • R: this package, cfcompare, an independent implementation that is not affiliated with the authors of the paper.

The implementations make different choices where the paper leaves room (how weights are anchored when many cells are treated, how penalties are cross-validated, how inference is done), and those choices change between releases. This page records them as dated snapshots: each table describes the four implementations as they stood at that date, and older snapshots are kept unchanged so that the evolution stays visible. Jump to the latest snapshot.

What changed between July and October 2026

Python trop

  • v0.1.10 (July 2026): Monte Carlo simulation tools that generate panels from features of a real dataset, to compare estimators; the estimator objective rewritten with cvxpy.sum_squares.
  • v0.1.11 (September 2026): unit-level bootstrap inference, trop.bootstrap (controls-only resampling by default, or stratified). The repository moved to zhaonanq/TROP-Estimator.

Stata trop

  • v0.2.6 (August 2026): in the pooled group(time) mode, unit distances now mask the other treated units and the target periods; new pooled_treat_distance(unit() time()) option to override a group’s distance to itself.
  • v0.2.7 (August 2026): adaptive cross-validation search, vce(jackknife), progress bars.
  • v0.2.8 (August 2026): the adaptive search starts with a sweep of the full grids.
  • v0.2.9 (September 2026): in group(time), the treated units are masked from the fit and the effect is estimated from the residual.

cfcompare

  • 0.2.0 (October 2026): pooled anchoring per treatment spell (Stata’s group(time) estimands, with per-spell effects in fit$tau_groups); pooled time weights centred on the spell midpoint; pooled_treat_distance; controls-only bootstrap resampling; delete-one-unit jackknife over every unit. See the changelog for details.
  • 0.2.1 (October 2026): this website; the comparison tables moved here from the README.

Numerical agreement with the official Python package

The TROP engine in cfcompare is written in base R. For correctness checks it has been compared with the official Python trop package on exactly comparable weighted-TWFE sample datasets, using trop_control(svd = "full"), and the results agree to numerical tolerance. The matrix-in entry point trop_matrix() keeps the Python package’s signature and conventions for such cross-checks.

Notes on cfcompare’s implementation choices

Solver. Finite nuclear-norm penalties are solved with a proximal-gradient soft-impute routine, as opposed to FISTA or SCS, so that the implementation depends only on base R; exact digits therefore need not match convex-solver implementations. To reconcile the difference, fix the penalties via lambda = list(time =, unit =, nn =) (bypassing cross-validation), set trop_control(svd = "full"), and match the other implementation’s anchoring.

Cross-validation. Penalties are chosen by leave-one-control-cell-out prediction error by default (the paper’s criterion); a placebo criterion that resamples the actual treatment patterns is available via trop_control(cv_method = "placebo"), and is the recommended choice under staggered adoption.

Per-cell or pooled anchoring. anchor = "per_cell" solves a separate locally weighted problem for each treated cell. anchor = "pooled" uses one set of weights per treatment spell group – treated cells with the same start and end period, pooled across units, the group(time) estimands of the Stata command – and is faster. Under block adoption there is one group; under staggered adoption one per cohort; a unit that switches in and out of treatment contributes one group per spell. A group’s unit distance is to the average path of its units over the periods in which none of them is treated, each comparison unit’s own treated cells are masked, and the time weights are centred on the spell midpoint. The per-group effects are returned in fit$tau_groups, and the ATT is their cell-weighted average. trop_control(pooled_treat_distance = list(unit = 0, time = 0)) gives the group’s own units and periods the full weight (the Stata command’s pooled_treat_distance()). trop_matrix() is always pooled over a single trailing block (the Python signature).

Covariates. Time-varying covariates can be supplied to trop() and panel_compare(); they enter the low-rank term additively, as in Section 6.2 of the paper.

Nuclear-norm floor. For numerical stability, the solver adds a small scale-relative floor to every finite lambda_nn by default (the reported lambda_nn does not include it). lambda_nn = Inf (the DID/TWFE-like case) is never affected, and trop_control(nn_floor = 0) applies the penalties exactly as supplied.

Standardization. Estimation uses the raw outcome by default, so lambda values are on the outcome’s natural scale; trop(standardize = TRUE) standardizes the outcome as the Stata command does, and then reports lambda on the standardized scale.

Inference. se = "bootstrap" resamples units with replacement, keeping each unit’s full time series: treated and control units separately by default (the stratified block bootstrap of the paper and of the Stata command), or only the control units with trop_control(boot_resample = "controls") (the default of the Python package’s trop.bootstrap). se = "jackknife" deletes one unit at a time over every unit, as the Stata command’s vce(jackknife); replicates that leave no treated unit are skipped.
